keyVerseText: When Jesus came into the coasts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?
rootMeaning: The word Καισάρεια (Kaisáreia) is derived from Καῖσαρ (Kaîsar), meaning 'Caesar,' the title of the Roman emperor. This etymology reveals that the name literally means 'place of Caesar' or 'belonging to Caesar,' indicating a city named in honor of the Roman imperial authority. This root sense adds a layer of historical and political significance beyond the simple English gloss 'Caesarea,' highlighting the city's connection to Roman rule and governance during the New Testament period.
usageInScripture: Καισάρεια appears 17 times in the New Testament and is consistently translated as 'Caesarea' or 'of Caesarea,' referring to two distinct locations in Palestine: Caesarea Philippi and Caesarea on the sea coast. The majority of occurrences (15 times) use the simple place name 'Caesarea,' emphasizing its geographical and historical identity. This consistent translation underscores the importance of these cities as notable centers within the biblical narrative, serving as key settings for events in the early church and Jesus' ministry.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Καισάρεια as a city named after Caesar enriches our comprehension of the New Testament context, where the gospel was proclaimed under the shadow of Roman imperial power. It reminds believers that the message of Christ transcended earthly authorities and kingdoms, confronting and transforming the world shaped by Caesar's rule. The presence of these cities in Scripture highlights God's sovereignty over all human governments and the call for Christians to witness faithfully within diverse political realities. Recognizing the imperial origin of the name invites reflection on the contrast between worldly power and the kingdom of God revealed in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 16:13, Jesus comes to the region of Caesarea Philippi and asks His disciples about the public perception of His identity. The mention of 'Caesarea Philippi' situates this pivotal theological question within a city bearing the name of the Roman emperor, underscoring the tension between earthly authority and the divine identity of Jesus. The word Καισάρεια here deepens the narrative by highlighting that Jesus' true kingship is questioned and contrasted against the backdrop of imperial power, inviting believers to recognize Him as the Son of Man beyond any earthly title or rule.
